author: Luca Tavan
title: How the Socialist Party is different from the other parties
content:
Members of the Socialist Party are often asked what makes us different from other parties. Prospective left-wing voters bruised by the long history of politicians selling out their principles want to know how we will avoid becoming part of the same establishment we want to challenge. On the other hand, some left-wing Greens question whether the Socialist Party is even necessary, seeing as their party already offers similar policies. 

The only way to answer these questions properly is to explain how the Socialist Party is unlike any other in Australian politics. We have a vision of society and a political strategy that differs fundamentally from all pro-capitalist parties, from the Liberals to the Greens. So what’s so distinctive about our project? 

Socialism!

The first thing is in the name. We are a socialist party, avowedly opposed to the whole capitalist system. Of course, the meaning of the term “socialism” is contested. Many progressive politicians, from UK Greens’ Zack Polanski to New York’s Zohran Mamdani, have ridden a wave of hostility toward right-wing billionaires and use the term “socialism” to describe their goal of reformed capitalism. 

But we don’t just want to tinker with the system: the Socialist Party wants to get rid of capitalism. We oppose an economy based on private business ownership and the exploitation of workers. We support a democratic, socialised

author: Barry York
title: From student activism to Pentridge and beyond: the life of Barry York
content:
Barry York was a leading student radical at La Trobe University at the height of the movement against the Vietnam War. In 1972, along with two other student activists, Barry was arrested and held in Pentridge Prison for his anti-war activity. He recently self-published a memoir of his time in Pentridge as a political prisoner which will soon be available at Red Flag books.

The La Trobe struggle was part of the wider student movement opposing the Vietnam War, conscription and apartheid in the late 1960s and early 1970s. On campus, we challenged the university’s ties to political and economic power, including Chancellor Sir Archibald Glenn’s association with ICI (Imperial Chemical Industries, renamed Orica Limited in 1998), which had contracts with the government linked to the Vietnam War. ICI’s parent company also had links to the munitions and chemicals industries in apartheid South Africa. We opposed La Trobe’s rule barring students suspended elsewhere from enrolling, and questioned its possible cooperation with the Joint Intelligence Organisation. At the heart of these campaigns was a basic question: whose interests should a university serve?

At a mass student meeting in April 1971, attended by about 1,000 people, students endorsed demands for action on these issues. It must be noted that, at that time, La Trobe was a small campus and probably only had about 1,500 students

author: Robert Narai
title: France’s student revolt
content:
Video footage shows tens of thousands of school students packed into Place de la République in Paris, chanting, “High schools in struggle! Youth on fire! The revolution is on the march!” It’s 6 October, and outside Lamartine high school, students hold placards that read, “More class hours than sleep” and “8am to 6pm, are we students or in police custody?”

“We are protesting because we deserve the right to have a good life”, Lyna tells 

Red Flag

 via text from the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis. She is a 16-year-old 

lycéenne

 (high schooler aged 15 to 18) at Paul-Éluard; her parents are Algerian immigrants. Lyna says many young people like her have lost faith that school will lead anywhere. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s budget proposes €54 billion in public spending cuts and the abolition of 1,588 teaching posts. Combined with police who treat young people from the 

banlieues

 (working-class suburbs) like 

racaille

 (“scum”) and a growing far right, it has created a disaffected layer of young people.

“There are cockroaches and rats everywhere”, Lyna says of her classrooms. “We have classes that go from 8am to 6pm. The police harass us on the streets because of the colour of our skin and the 

banlieue

 we live in. We, the children of the 

banlieues

, are abandoned and neglected.” Yet students in better parts of Paris have joined Lyna. “We know we’re

author: Ridah Hassan
title: Manosphere making classrooms toxic
content:
“I had male students threatening to rape the female students consistently. They would play ‘rape marry kill’ and used my own name frequently in their ‘game’.”

“Students saying ‘good girl’ to teachers.”

“Less respect for female staff vs male in behaviour—even with the same approaches they instantly listen to males more. More inappropriate jokes—racism, homophobic and sexist jokes with little consequences. Visible [and] audible dismissal/rejection of female staff to their faces when they appear to take classes.” 

These are quotes from a Monash University report which has cast light on the disturbing sexist conditions faced by teachers and students in primary and secondary schools across the country. 

Duty of Care: Teachers’ experiences of sexism, misogyny and sexual harassment in Australian schools

 is based on the testimony of 2,600 educators and reveals the breadth and depth of the crisis. 

A common theme in the report is the lack of respect male students show female teachers. This includes frequent interrupting, ignoring of instructions, mocking and mimicking, speaking disrespectfully and refusing to accept responsibility when challenged about inappropriate behaviour. Physical aggression and intimidation were also reported, along with threats of more serious physical and sexual assault. author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Westsiders campaign against AI hub
content:
I met Anthony and Samantha on Holden Road in Plumpton, 40 kilometres west of Melbourne’s CBD. We’ve parked our cars at the Melbourne Renewable Energy hub gate, behind which a huge expanse of land could become home to a hyperscale data centre owned and operated by Syncline Energy. 

The surrounding area is a green wedge, meaning that it should be protected from industrial and urban sprawl. There’s a free-range egg farm, rolling fields, some houses and a few horses. Samantha, who is campaigning against the development, lives five minutes away in Diggers Rest and learned to ride a horse right here. In fact, one we are looking at is called Betsy and is the very same horse. 

A 

petition

 against the AI hub raises concerns about environmental destruction, including “endangered ecological vegetation communities, biodiversity corridors, areas of Aboriginal cultural heritage sensitivity and conservation efforts”.

The Plumpton plan is still awaiting approval from the state government. If it gets it, the site will host a

 

350-hectare AI hub

, which the 

Age

 reports is the size of 175 MCG playing fields. The facility will have a maximum power draw of 2.5 gigawatts, more than the entire output of the Loy Yang A coal power plant. Loy Yang A provides around 

30 percent of Victoria’s power

. It would use more power than every other data centre currently operating combined.

author: Ella Gutteridge
title: Hundreds protest far-right conference in Brisbane
content:
High-profile racists and far-right leaders descended on the Brisbane showgrounds over the weekend of 10 and 11 October for the Conservative Political Action Conference.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson headlined the event. She was joined by Liberal leader Angus Taylor, far-right podcaster Karl Stefanovic, and one of Britain’s least successful politicians, former Prime Minister Liz Truss.

Inside, it was a carnival of reaction. The ABC reported that 

Hanson was greeted with 

rapturous applause

 as she harangued the Coalition for signing up to net-zero and creating an eSafety commissioner, which she pledged to abolish on the grounds of free speech.

The leader of the National Party, Matt Canavan, cosplayed as a blue-collar worker as he took to the stage to extol the virtues of Australian manufacturing. Despite earlier criticisms, Hanson said that she’d be willing to work with the Coalition to “

throw out this wretched and corrupt Labor government

”.

Outside, hundreds of irreverent high schoolers, trade union activists and community members rallied, waving homemade signs, chanting and drumming. The crowd was a sea of keffiyehs, rainbow flags and signs, with many commenting on Hanson’s close relationship with Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart (“Pauline works for Gina!”).

author: April Holcombe
title: Chinese youth in a very shit time of their lives
content:
Certain quarters of the internet are filling with content lauding contemporary China as an advanced, anti-imperialist, even socialist society. Its unrivalled high-speed rail network and its continued use of Communist jargon have encouraged some disillusioned Western youth to declare themselves in “a very Chinese time of my life”.

State-of-the-art infrastructure and Communist iconography have obvious appeal to a section of people living in decaying, imperialist and increasingly far-right-controlled Western capitalism. But there is a big difference between Instagram China, a Potemkin country showcased by influencers at the invitation of the tourism bureau and marketed to disillusioned Western youth, and the real China, a nuclear superpower ruled by bureaucrat-businessmen.  

Young Chinese people on social media—students, workers and the unemployed—use a very different kind of language than influencers do. Theirs is the language of alienation, exploitation and oppression in a society every bit as capitalist as our own.

“Involution”: an obscure word for a common problem

Ever heard of “involution”? Me neither. This obscure academic term, translated into Chinese (内卷 

neijuan

author: Priya T.
title: Eugene Debs—the socialist who won a million votes
content:
Eugene Debs was the most popular and beloved socialist leader in United States history. Famed for exceptional speechmaking, the Socialist Party of America raised $20,000 to buy a train for Debs’ inaugural run for president in 1906. The “Red Special” carried Debs across the country to hundreds of meetings, from the union halls of mining towns to a mass gathering of more than 10,000 workers at New York’s Madison Square Garden. 

A lifetime of struggle, and the lessons born from bitter defeats, transformed Debs from a trade unionist and Democrat to a socialist committed to building a working-class party. 

Debs was born in 1855 in the small town of Terre Haute in Indiana. At fourteen, he started working on the railroads. Railways were central to the industrial expansion going on in the United States at the time, connecting major cities and transporting commodities between them. Capitalists employed gangster violence against unions, keeping working conditions dangerous and wages pitiful. Ray Ginger, in his famous 1949 biography of Debs, writes that in his fifth year on the railways, a friend and workmate of Debs fell under a train and died. Worried he’d meet the same all-too-common fate, Debs returned to Terre Haute shortly afterwards.

author: Connor Knight
title: When Australian socialists dared to dream
content:
In the years after World War One, the Australian socialist movement reached its peak influence. Socialists led big strikes, gave speeches to crowds of tens of thousands and oversaw a flourishing radical press. Thousands of workers believed socialism was possible. But until now, few historians have given this generation of Australian socialists the acknowledgement they deserve. 

Duncan Hart has been a prominent socialist in Brisbane for nearly two decades. 

His new book

, 

From Revolutionary Hopes to Shattered Dreams: The Socialist Movement in Australia:1918-1925,

 brings this momentous period of Australian socialism to life—its revolutionary promise, the fierce debates that animated it and its eventual decline. He spoke to 

Red Flag

’s Connor Knight in Brisbane about the book. 

What inspired you to write this book? 

I was inspired at first by reading some of the history on the period that did already exist. I started to get the sense that it was a much more significant period than it has been given credit for. I was inspired by reading about the people in the movement—they were genuine socialists who wanted to overthrow capitalism, not supporters of dictatorships or advocates of gradual reform. 

Your book covers the period directly after World War One. How did the war affect life in Australia, and how did it contribute to the growth of the socialist and workers’ movem

author: Gabby Soltura
title: University workers on strike in Brisbane
content:
National Tertiary Education Union members from Brisbane’s three major universities rallied in Queens Gardens on 8 October during a simultaneous 

half-day strike

. After walking out at 11am, staff from the University of Queensland, Queensland University of Technology and Griffith University gathered in the city, chanting, “Chop from the top”! and “Union power”!

The popularity of the “chop from the top” slogan shouldn’t surprise anyone; QUT and UQ vice-chancellors 

Margaret Shiel

 and 

Deborah Terry

 both took home whopping $1.2 million salaries in 2025. Across the street from the rally stood a symbol of the bosses’ greed: Brisbane’s Treasury Building, which 

Griffith recently bought for $67 million

, despite not having enough office space for staff. While vice-chancellors live in luxury and splurge on real estate, the workers who make our universities run are being offered crumbs.

UQ management’s most recent wage offer is 

15.5 percent over 4 years

, or 3.9 percent per year, lower than current and projected inflation. Matthew Campbell, UQ branch vice-president and national councillor, told the rally that this offer would drive workers into rental stress. Management at 

QUT

 and 

Griffith

 have so far refused to present a pay offer.

Along with wage increases, the workers want secure jobs and sustainable working conditions.

author: Deaglan Godwin
title: NSW Socialists launch campaign with a bang!
content:
“Our message is clear: the working class isn’t going to take this shit lying down anymore”, roared Ryan Chapman, NSW Socialists candidate for the seat of Wollongong, at the launch of the party’s 2027 state election campaign.

The 300-strong crowd burst out in applause. The venue, Ashfield Town Hall, was packed to capacity.

The speakers, three of the party’s six lower-house candidates, reflected Australia’s modern, multicultural working class. The first speaker, Alma Torlakovic, candidate for the Western Sydney seat of Granville, spoke movingly of her childhood in war-torn Bosnia and Croatia. Shovan Bhattarai, candidate for the inner-west seat of Newtown, humorously described the multicultural lunchtimes at her Western Sydney primary school. Chapman spoke of growing up working class on the South Coast and joining the navy as his only option.

The housing crisis was a recurring theme. Chapman spoke about the campaign to defend the Bellambi housing estate north of Wollongong. Labor MP for the area and state planning minister Paul Scully wants to knock down the estate because it is on prized beachfront property. After detailing the eye-watering average rent rises in the inner-west, Bhattarai explained the party’s housing policy of slashing rents by 35 percent, implementing a rent freeze and building 150,000 new public housing units.

author: Tom Sullivan
title: Housing protests lead to general strike in Spain
content:
“I haven’t managed to defend my house, but I have tried so that others can learn how to defend theirs.” These were the words of an 87-year-old Madrid woman, Maricarmen, who posted a video from her hospital bed after Spanish authorities evicted her from the apartment she had lived in for the past 71 years. In the video, she promoted an upcoming protest at Madrid’s Plaza del Sol “so that we can eliminate this problem once and for all”.

Her eviction sparked a fire across the Spanish state. Within days, protesters had set up an encampment in the Plaza del Sol, famously the site of mass anti-austerity protests in 2011. They quickly spread to dozens of other cities, along with mass protests. A few days later came the first victory of the movement, when the vulture fund that had bought Maricarmen’s apartment building agreed to allow her to return with a new, eight-year contract and her rent capped at 30 percent of her pension.

But this victory only fuelled the protests. On Saturday 3 October, nationally coordinated rallies saw around half a million people protest across the country. Three days later, the country’s two major union confederations called a general strike.

author: Lance Selfa
title: What’s up with Jacobin’s “Working-Class Win-o-Meter”?
content:
Every few months, 

Jacobin 

magazine announces what it purports to be a secret to win working-class voters based on a finding from its associated Center for Working Class Politics (CWCP). Its 14 September editorial “

Report: The Working Class Vote is Not Lost

” was the latest in this series.

CWCP’s latest innovation is the “Working-Class Win-o-Meter”, which Jacobin describes as “a data-driven road map for winning back working-class voters”. It purports to demonstrate the optimal combination of social and political appeals to move working-class voters to vote for a hypothetical Democratic candidate.

Two points should be made at the outset. When

 Jacobin

 and CWCP talk about “winning working class voters,” they don’t mean winning the working class to socialism. They mean “winning” the working class to vote for Democrats. And they define the “working class” as non-college-educated people with family incomes of between $30,000 and $150,000.

This supposedly groundbreaking survey and analysis is an exercise in political message-testing for Democratic candidates. It uses the definition of “working-class” that is the standard in lazy polling and media commentary, and thus adds no new insights. Attaching the labels of “socialist” and “working-class” doesn’t change the fact that what

 Jacobin

 and CWCP are engaged in is a completely conventional activity that regularly earns m

author: Yuanyi Tham
title: Mega Anthropic data centre to blight Queensland
content:
Queensland is set to become home to Australia’s largest AI data centre. Last month, Liberal National Party Premier David Crisafulli announced a landmark deal with Anthropic to develop the Western Downs Digital Park, near the town of Dalby, about 250 kilometres northwest of Brisbane. Led by Singaporean developer Zerra DC, the site will be constructed in four phases, with the first building expected to be operational next year.

The data centre will occupy 725.5 hectares, an area twice the size of New York’s Central Park. Its estimated value is $32 billion, nearly five times the 2032 Brisbane Olympics infrastructure budget.

Data centres suck up huge amounts of power, driving up energy prices and accelerating climate change. When fully constructed, electro-mechanical engineer Dr Andreas Helwig told the ABC it would use the equivalent of 25 to 30 percent of Queensland’s total energy consumption.

The data centre will run primarily on electricity generated by coal and gas, drawn from the state’s electricity grid. Greenpeace estimates that the data centre would raise the grid’s emissions by 6.6 million tonnes, the equivalent of two million extra cars on the road.

Last month, Crisafulli wrestled with the federal government and eventually won a state exemption from the requirement that data centres run on renewable energy. The exemption, Crisafulli argued, was simply “common sense”;

author: Mary Ellen Murphy
title: Hospital doctors strike for wages, safe hours and public health
content:
In July, Victorian public hospital doctors voted 97 percent in favour of taking industrial action for the first time in 20 years. The reason is simple: the healthcare system is unsafe for patients and staff.

The Victorian healthcare system is in crisis. Systemic failures at every level compound one another. Limited access to primary care and community services leaves people more unwell and reliant on emergency departments for care. This results in long wait times, overcrowding and unsafe workloads.

Bed shortages, often caused by delays in discharging patients due to the lack of support services, are also an issue. For example, recent data from the Victorian Health Department shows that nineteen of 21 mental health units fail to admit acutely unwell patients from the emergency department within eight hours. This results in staff attempting to care for patients in under-resourced and unsuitable environments in which they are at greater risk of violence. The lack of suitable facilities for mental health patients and adequate staffing also contributes to the ongoing failures to meet goals for the reduction in use of restrictive interventions such as seclusion and restraint.

It is no wonder then that burnout is endemic among public hospital doctors like me working in this broken system. We are expected to be machines and cope with unsafe workloads, under-resourcing and excessive

author: Vashti Fox
title: Three years of Palestine solidarity
content:
In mid-October 2023, after the first major march against Israel’s attacks on Gaza, the director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign UK, Ben Jamal, said to his staff: “We are probably going to need to be responding to this through marches until potentially Christmas”. He was wrong. The protests did not abate. As Israel’s offensive in Gaza continued, the number of actions across the world multiplied rapidly, eventually blossoming into one of the largest and most sustained antiwar movements in generations. From the world’s largest cities to the smallest hamlets, millions of voices rose in the same chant, with the same cadence: “Free, free Palestine!” 

The numbers tell part of the story. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), an international monitor, estimated that, in the three weeks after 7 October, some 3,700 demonstrations calling for a ceasefire and showing solidarity with Palestine took place in almost 100 countries and territories. In the first months of the genocide, most were in the Middle East and North Africa and were especially frequent in Yemen, Iran, Turkey and Morocco. In several of these countries, major government or religious institutions backed the demonstrations. 

In the West, however, governments were overwhelmingly hostile. In France, for instance, pro-Israel demonstrations were legal and encouraged. But the Macron government banned all

author: Editors
title: The world since 7 October
content:
Gaza is a generational touchstone and the key dividing line of politics in the West. It has laid bare the lies of the society we live in. It has exposed the genocidal bloodlust of the political right. And it has tested official “progressive” liberal politics, which has so often shown itself to be utterly hollow or cowardly. 

Anyone can now use Google Maps’ satellite view to see for themselves the apocalypse wrought by Israel and its allies over the past three years. Gaza City, once home to around 700,000 people, is a mostly bombed-out hellscape of ruins. The same is true of Beit Hanoun, Jabalia and other major centres. 

Rafah was a city thousands of years old, first recorded in an inscription from 1303 BCE. It has now been wiped off the face of the earth. Google still displays location markers for what once existed: “Kamal Adwan School”, “Playground”, “Musab bin Amir Western Mosque”, now a pile of rubble—“temporarily closed”, according to Google.

About 80 percent of structures in the Gaza Strip have been damaged; two-thirds of those are destroyed, according to the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees. Israel has used the so-called ceasefire since last December to systematically demolish remaining structures in the 60 percent of the Strip occupied by its forces, while killing another 1,200 Palestinians and herding around 2 million into unliveable tent cities in an e

author: Nick Everett
title: How the media sold the Gaza genocide
content:
When 700,000 Rohingya were forced to flee Myanmar for Bangladesh amid widespread killings, sexual violence and village burnings in late 2017, an 

Age 

editorial pleaded for Australian government action: 

“There is a genocide happening today in Myanmar. Our government should urgently, repeatedly and loudly call for international intervention, and lead in imposing sanctions. We should send bountiful aid to the victims, and halt economic and diplomatic relations with Myanmar unless and until the savagery is stopped. All of us, as Australians, should shun travel to Myanmar for tourism or business. And our government should, as it did with the Syrian refugee crisis a few years ago, rapidly engineer an intake of Rohingya refugees.”

The 

Age

 didn’t wait for an International Court of Justice ruling before issuing its dire warning. It repeatedly used the term “genocide” to describe the Myanmar state’s atrocities despite no case of genocide having been brought before the ICJ at the time (it wasn’t until late 2019 that Gambia brought such a case and the ICJ still hasn’t ruled on it).

After three years of Israeli genocide in Gaza, no similar editorial can be found in the 

Age

, nor in any of the mainstream media in Australia. That is despite Israel having killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, including over 21,280 children who, 

according to

 a UN Commission of inquiry, have be

author: Emily Lassam
title: French high school students on the march
content:
“I like this kinda thing because it’s revolutionary”, a 16-year-old high school student told me as we stood out the front of her school in Nice at 7am on the last Wednesday in September. As we talked, students started arriving from across the city to join the blockade of the school, the Lycée Parc Imperial, the largest in the area.

Hundreds of students trickled in, and suddenly it was hard to tell where the sea of high schoolers started and ended. Some carried things to help build the barricades to stop anyone from entering the school.

I asked the 16-year-old if she knew all the students or whether they were from other schools. She pointed out a group of high schoolers who must have travelled from another school and said: “I don’t know them, but we are all comrades”.

This wasn’t the first blockade she had been part of at this school, but she said it was different to previous blockades. This time, it isn’t just one school but more than 1,000 being blockaded.

Videos and photos of French students holding Palestinian and Algerian flags, calling for revolution, chanting against the far-right National Rally and fighting against intense repression are sweeping social media.

This comes at a moment when a growing wave of student protests and revolts is sweeping across the world. Last year, there were the Gen Z revolts that were led by students and swept across Nepal, Indonesia, Mad

author: Cormac Mills Ritchard
title: Demolishing the idea of public housing
content:
The United Nations’ special rapporteur on adequate housing, Koldo Casla, usually deals with slum demolitions in third-world countries. Last month, he took aim at the Victorian Labor government, claiming its demolition of Melbourne’s 44 public housing towers and the “forced evictions and mass displacement of approximately 10,000 residents” could be a violation of their 

human rights

. This follows a Victorian parliamentary inquiry in December, which called for an 

immediate pause

 to the demolitions, and a class action against the demolitions filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal (IMCL), which has been granted special leave to 

appeal

 to the High Court on 7 October.

Despite growing challenges, Premier Ben Carroll is ploughing ahead with the demolition of Melbourne’s public housing towers. Of course, Labor doesn’t characterise what it’s doing as “eviction” and “demolition”, but “renewal” and “redevelopment”, which it claims will increase the number of residents on the estates from 10,000 to 30,000, and replace towers that have “reached the end of their useful life”. There is no truth to this.

If Labor’s multi-billion-dollar project is aimed at addressing the waiting list for social housing, it’s missing a couple of zeros. Only 11,000 of the new residents will be in social housing, an increase of just 1,000. As of June this year, there were 58,021 people on the Victori

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: Germany’s far right surges
content:
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains in several state elections across Germany in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, the party won a frightening 44 percent of the vote and fell just three seats short of forming government. Two weeks later, it won 38 percent in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, doubling its vote share from the previous election. Even in liberal, multicultural Berlin, the AfD vote went from 9 percent to 16 percent.

The results have sent political shockwaves across not just across Germany but the whole of Europe. It is no wonder why. The AfD is on the extreme wing of the broader far-right surge worldwide. Founded in 2013 as a Eurosceptic opposition to Chancellor Angela Merkel’s bailouts of the Greek government, the party has moved radically to the right over the last decade.

Today, the AfD calls for mass deportations and a strict blood-based concept of German citizenship, while opposing the right to political asylum. It also campaigns for separate schools for the children of migrants. The party also argues that focusing on the crimes of the Nazi period encourages national humiliation and therefore opposes Holocaust memorials. In 2023, AfD leaders attended a secret meeting in Potsdam with wealthy donors and prominent neo-Nazis to develop a plan to expel from the country millions of migrants and refugees and hundreds of thousands of German citizens o

author: Deaglan Godwin
title: Student Union independence under threat at Sydney University
content:
The University of Sydney has announced its intention to intervene in the student union and potentially undermine democratic elections.

The announcement follows a controversy, concocted by the right-wing Murdoch media, about an election ticket contesting this year’s Students’ Representative Council election. The ticket, called Globalise the Intifada, drew hysterical condemnation from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, federal Education Minister Jason Clare and a spokesperson for NSW Premier Chris Minns. Albanese told Sydney’s 

Daily Telegraph

 the slogan “is an absolute outrage that has no place in Australia”. 

Vice-chancellor Mark Scott and chancellor David Thodey joined the chorus of condemnation. 

In a statement released on 29 September

, they said: “We deplore the manipulation of the recent election campaign to spread hurtful and distressing language across campus”. 

The university also said it will commission an independent review of the SRC’s “current affiliation and funding arrangements ... to ensure compliance with legal, regulatory, and psychosocial safety requirements”. The review will also focus on student and staff codes of conduct and on campus security. 

Behind closed doors, Scott and Thodey floated even more drastic measures. A source present at last week’s University Senate meeting 

told 

Honi Soit

, the student newspaper, that Scott raised the possibili

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: On the campaign trail with Victorian Socialists
content:
“We need Jasmine in parliament!”, called out Abdul. He runs Konjo, an Ethiopian cafe in Footscray. He’d just let us use the cafe as a backdrop for a promotional video we were making for the Victorian Socialists’ state election campaign. I’m running as the party’s candidate for the Western Metropolitan upper house region, and the cafe is adorned with a huge picture of Jasmine Duff, our candidate for Footscray. It is one of hundreds of campaign signs on front fences and on stakes in people’s front yards across the electorate. 

Since the last federal election, it feels like support for Victorian Socialists has grown. Back then, Jasmine was the candidate for the federal seat of Fraser—encompassing Footscray and suburbs to the west and south, including Yarraville, Sunshine and St Albans. At the booth I staffed, and have done for the last few election cycles, she received more than 20 percent of the vote. In Seddon, the booth at the scout hall recorded 18 percent for Jasmine. 

Near that scout hall, I recently met a woman who had always voted Green. She told me she had volunteered with Sea Shepherd in her youth and cared deeply about the environment, as well as sexism in our society. We talked about how society is getting worse. We talked about the fear of heading into an El Niño at the same time as the government has just fast-tracked the development of the NextDC hyperscale data c

author: Danica Rachel
title: Protest called against October arms fair in Perth
content:
The Land Forces Exposition 2026, to be held at the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre on 6-8 October, will be a three-day extravaganza of exhibitions, talks and luncheons, where the main topic of conversation is how best to kill people. More than 20,000 weapons company executives, politicians and military personnel from around the world are expected to attend.

We have to protest against this outrageous celebration of death and destruction.

Photos from the 2024 event on the front page of the 

Land Forces website

 are enough to make you ill. A smiling representative of Anduril, a company specialising in AI-powered warfare, shows off a battle drone. A live demonstration of a robot dog, presumably designed to carry autonomous weapons, takes place on the exhibition floor. A drone as big as a car hangs from the ceiling.

Lockheed Martin, the world’s biggest arms dealer—and builder of the F-35 fighter jets Israel uses to bomb Gaza—will have its latest death machines on display. As will Elbit Systems, Israel’s biggest weapons company.

Senior executives from Anduril and BAE Systems will speak on a panel discussing “the realities of Ukraine, Iran and other current conflicts”. Today’s bloodshed used as a case study to make tomorrow’s killing more efficient. What could those “other conflicts” be? Israel’s invasion of Lebanon? One assumes that there’s much these monsters have learn

author: James Plested
title: Victorian Socialists’ election campaign in full swing
content:
The Victorian state election will take place in just over two months, on Saturday 28 November. The Victorian Socialists’ campaign is now in full swing, with local campaign activity taking place daily across Melbourne and regional Victoria.

The scale of the campaign—with VS candidates set to run in all 88 lower house seats and all eight upper house regions across Victoria—is beyond anything the socialist left in Australia has attempted for generations (if ever). Even just a few years ago, a statewide campaign like this would have been unthinkable. That it’s happening at all is something of a breakthrough.

Between 1 June and 19 September, VS volunteers knocked on more than 80,000 doors, already well on track to reach the 2022 campaign total of around 190,000. The party received around 2,000 requests for campaign signs to be put on front fences and in yards, eclipsing the 2022 total of 1,000, with hundreds of orders a week still coming in. More than 2,400 people donated to the campaign, and almost 1,800 registered for a party event. 

New branches are springing up everywhere. Wherever they do, we’re finding people who want to get involved. VS events in places like Pakenham, a suburb on the far south-eastern fringe of Melbourne—more than 50 kilometres from the CBD—are attracting many new faces. author: Tom Bramble
title: What’s the deal with productivity?
content:
The bosses are trying to convince workers that lower corporate taxes, fewer regulations and workers’ rights, and less union power would be good for real wages. What they really want is more profits at the expense of the working class.

For years, business lobby groups have decried what they call Australia’s “productivity crisis”. They don’t say workers are producing less than they used to; they say they aren’t increasing production as quickly as before and aren’t keeping pace with overseas productivity growth.

It’s true: growth in workers’ hourly output has slowed over the past decade, and Australian workers don’t produce as much value for the bosses as American workers. But the bosses argue that this means living standards are held back, and prices rise more than they otherwise would, contributing to the cost-of-living crisis.

They say that government regulations (rules about wages, hours of work, health and safety standards, construction standards, environmental protections and professional and occupational registration requirements) and trade unions are preventing business investment. Their solution is “deregulation”, “slashing red tape”, “more competition”. These are simply code words for attacking the working class.

author: Emma Black
title: Strangulation: How did attempted murder become normal?
content:
A 16-year-old woman from Sydney’s northern beaches died in hospital in late August after reportedly being strangled during consensual sex with her partner. The tragedy has sparked a long-overdue reckoning with the consequences for young women of the pornification of sex and the normalisation of sexual violence that has come with it.

In recent years, sexual strangulation has gone from being a relatively marginal phenomenon to an everyday sexual practice. In Australia, 61 percent of young women report having been strangled during sex, according to a 

2024 survey

 of thousands of 18- to 35-year-olds. Men are most likely to be the stranglers. There is no safe way to strangle someone. According to David Corlett and Marie Crabbe, founders of anti-strangulation advocacy group Breathless:

“Potential 

consequences

 [of strangulation] 

range from

 neck pain to loss of bladder and bowel control, headaches, memory loss, seizures, brain damage, stroke and, as seems to be the case with the young woman from the northern beaches, death. The risks and consequences are cumulative, so the more someone is strangled, the more likely they are to suffer harm.”

author: Lucy Chapman-Kelly
title: ‘Rig your own stages!’: Melbourne theatre workers strike
content:
Fans of Macy Gray were met by hundreds of Arts Centre Melbourne staff on strike for the first time in the institution’s history on 11 September. More than 95 percent of union members

 voted

 in favour of the 24-hour strike, rejecting management’s 3 percent offer and instead demanding an above-inflation pay rise, back pay from last October, and increased government funding for the arts.

According to the 

unions

 covering the workers—the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance and the Communications and Public Sector Union—Arts Centre staff wages have gone backwards in real terms by 10 percent since 2022, and almost 40 percent of the workforce is paid at the minimum award rate. Management’s 3 percent pay rise offer amounts to a further cut in real wages.

Nearly half the workforce is casual, and contact between workers is limited. Workers serving drinks at the bar, for example, might never interact with the ushers who seat people. The high turnover characteristic of casual work also means people don’t work with the same people consistently. This creates barriers to organising the workforce, and highlights why the strike, and the broader campaign for a better agreement, is a significant achievement.

author: Eleanor Morley
title: The problems of AI are the problems of capitalism
content:
Recent revelations about artificial intelligence models “going rogue” have raised serious concerns that the technology could soon cause great damage to human society. Already, the production and application of AI is wreaking havoc on the environment, amplifying existing social problems and expanding the powers of the surveillance state. While further regulation of the industry is necessary, the fundamental problem with AI is that capitalists control it and it is subject to the system’s prevailing conditions of profit maximisation, competition, imperial rivalry and more.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”, Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI, the world’s leading frontier AI model developers, wrote on X in early September. Anthropic’s chief safety researcher Evan Hubinger later responded similarly. “We do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans”, he wrote. “I personally think it is >10 percent within the next decade.”

Amid the myriad other doomsday scenarios the world faces—catastrophic weather and mass extinction events from climate change, the threat of inter-imperialist nuclear war, economic collapse and mass starvation and so on—this latest warning of impending catastrophe could get lost. author: Ruby Healer
title: Labor doubles down on US military alliance
content:
“American force posture in Australia is growing”, Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles declared on his visit to Washington, DC, this month. “Since we’ve come to government”, Marles said, standing alongside US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, “you can see a through line there of growing American force posture in Australia”.

It was a fairly straightforward summary of the Albanese Labor government’s attitude, followed up with promises of further integration between the Australian and US militaries. A shifting “force posture” will mean more American troop rotations, more US air and naval operations and more pre-positioning of military equipment like warplanes, fuel and munitions in Australia.

Agreements made by the Albanese government will ramp up co-operation on all fronts, with a newly 

revitalised

 HMAS Stirling base near Perth set to host American nuclear-powered submarines and an estimated 2,300 US troops within five years. As America’s military machine looks ahead to an era of aggressive contest with China in the Asia-Pacific, Australia’s ruling class is desperate to make itself an indispensable part of US war planning.

loosened

author: James McVicar
title: Why do the Greens always chicken out?
content:
When Larissa Waters was elected leader of the Australian Greens, she said she was there to “

get shit done

”.

True to her word, Waters did something last week—and it was, indeed, shit. Greens MPs gave 

crucial support

 in the Senate to the roll-out of a carbon emissions offset scheme so bad that the term “greenwashing” seems generous.

Under the scheme, state governments will now be able to take publicly owned forest, promise not to deforest it, and then convert that promise into “carbon credits”. These credits can then be sold to greenhouse gas emitters to subtract from their overall carbon emissions count.

In NSW, the scheme is being tied to the establishment of a 476,000-hectare koala reserve the state government had already promised back in 2015. This move, according to Larissa Waters, put the Greens in an “

impossible position

” and forced them to support Labor’s carbon credit scam.

So now, in exchange for doing something it had already said it would do, the NSW Labor government can continue to do 

nothing

 to trees that were 

already there

 and, in turn, magically generate permits for carbon emitters to carry on emitting carbon.

The Greens are now trying to sell this as a step forward for the planet, Waters describing it as the “first chink in the armour of coal and gas”.
